title: Rawls and the veil of ignorance
examples: What does it mean to not know your place in society?
How does this help us decide what rules are fair?
Can we really trust that we will be fair this way?

explain.say: John Rawls thought about how we make rules for a society.

draw.text: Rawls and the veil of ignorance

items: It helps us think about justice.
We decide rules without knowing our status.

explain.say: Imagine a group of people choosing rules for a new society.
This imaginary situation is called the veil of ignorance.
Because you do not know your place, you must choose fair rules.
For example, you would want rules that help the least fortunate people.
In everyday life, we see this when we make school rules.

faq.q: What exactly is the veil of ignorance?
faq.a: It is a thought experiment where you do not know your personal details. You do not know if you will be rich or poor.
asks: Is it a real thing or just an idea?

faq.q: Why do we use this idea for justice?
faq.a: It forces us to think about rules from a position of complete impartiality. We must design for the worst possible outcome.
asks: How does this help us be fair?
What is the purpose of the veil?

faq.q: Does this mean we should always help the poorest people?
faq.a: It suggests that the rules must protect the most vulnerable members of society. This ensures a basic level of fairness for everyone.
asks: Is helping the poor always the answer?
What is the main focus of the rules?

faq.q: Can we actually use this concept in real politics?
faq.a: It is a philosophical tool, not a direct law. It helps guide our thinking toward principles of fairness and equality.
asks: Is this just for talking about philosophy?

faq.a: The philosopher who developed this concept is John Rawls. He wrote about it to discuss social justice.
asks: Where did this idea come from?

facts: The veil of ignorance is a thought experiment.
It requires people to choose rules without knowing their own social standing.
The goal is to ensure the resulting rules are as fair as possible for everyone.
It emphasizes impartiality in the selection of societal laws.

quiz.say: If you are choosing rules and do not know if you will be healthy or sick, what principle guides your choice?

options.show: You would prioritize basic healthcare access for everyone.
options.say: You would prioritize basic healthcare access for everyone.

quiz.why: Because you might end up being the one who needs the most care.

wrong.0: This does not protect the basic needs of the most vulnerable people.
wrong.2: This ignores the possibility that you might be the one who is sick.
wrong.3: This would mean the rules are not fair to those who are poor now.

quiz.say: What does the veil of ignorance remove from the chooser?

options.show: It removes the concept of rules
options.say: It removes the concept of rules

options.show: It removes knowledge of your specific class or talents.
options.say: It removes knowledge of your specific class or talents.

quiz.why: This forces you to think about general fairness, not personal gain.

wrong.0: You are still in the process of choosing rules.
wrong.2: You still know the general rules of society.
wrong.3: You are still capable of making rational choices.

quiz.say: If a society has rules for education, what does the veil suggest about the rules?

options.show: The rules should only favor the talented
options.say: The rules should only favor the talented

options.show: The rules should be very expensive
options.say: The rules should be very expensive

options.show: The rules should be very basic
options.say: The rules should be very basic

options.show: The rules should guarantee a good baseline education for everyone.
options.say: The rules should guarantee a good baseline education for everyone.

quiz.why: If you don't know if you will be poor, you want good education available to you.

wrong.0: This creates unfair gaps based on unknown ability.
wrong.1: Expensive rules might only be affordable for some people.
wrong.2: This might not prepare you if you are lucky enough to be talented.
